audit.recode_to: No change of stress class. Fold chol1285 into chol1282 (the catalog's own identity_v42 ruling is MERGE-FOR-COUNTING, retired code cti -> ctu). If a Tila row is kept for display, re-pin it to Vázquez Álvarez 2011 §2.2 pp. 43-45 (+ 2002 §3 pp. 5-7) with rule window 2-8 / fixed-strict like chol1282, replace the carried quote with the rule sentence (Coon 2010:190 'Stress in Chol... is word final in declarative sentences' or VA 2011:43), and lift the grade from carried-secondary to primary-page-pinned.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: the audit record itself has no quote/cite; the upstream V44 quote (Coon 2010 App. A.2.2) is verbatim on p. 190 of the held PDF, but it is the interrogative/future-research sentence, not the rule sentence that sits two lines above it. (2) Deciding source: a 2010 MIT syntax dissertation's sketch appendix, second-hand from Vázquez Álvarez 2002; both it and the better sources describe Tila Chol, so there is no languoid mismatch — but chol1285 is a retired ISO split ([cti] merged into [ctu] 2009) and the chol1282 'Chol' record is built from Vázquez Álvarez 2011, whose data are also Tila Chol. The two rows are therefore the same variety coded twice from overlapping sources, with inconsistent windows (2-4 fixed-dominant here vs 2-8 fixed-strict there). (3) Substance: final word stress is stated independently by Vázquez Álvarez 2002:5-7 (paradigm to 6 syllables), Vázquez Álvarez 2011:

sources.citation: Bennett, Ryan. 2016. Mayan phonology. Language and Linguistics Compass 10(10): 469-514. doi:10.1111/lnc3.12148 (author PDF, people.ucsc.edu/~rbennett)
sources.quote: Fixed final stress is the Mayan norm outside Mamean/Yucatecan; 'Phrasal conditioning of various sorts has been reported for Mayan languages with fixed stress ... Similar patterns have been noted for Greater Tseltalan languages (Kaufman 1971, Attinasi 1973, Warkentin & Brend 1974, Haviland 1981, Coon 2010, Vázquez Álvarez 2011, Polian 2013)'; notes some putative phrase-level patterns 'may involve phrase-level intonational contours rather than true word-level stress' and that more investigation is needed. No instrumental study of Ch'ol stress is cited.

sources.citation: Vázquez Álvarez, Juan Jesús. 2011. A Grammar of Chol, a Mayan Language. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin. xx+519 pp. (open PDF, chol.lingspace.org; previously only in the session now copied to the audit folder)
sources.quote: 'In general, there is a main lexical stress in Chol which commonly falls on the last syllable of the word' (p. 43), with final-stressed examples of 1-3 syllables incl. loans (alaxáx, kixtyañúj); 'Compound forms also place the main stress on the last syllable' (p. 44); with added clitics 'the main stress moves toward the last syllable' up to buch-ul-oñ=tyo=ku=lá (p. 45); 'The main stress moves toward the first syllable when the speaker wants to make a yes/no question' (p. 45).
sources.locator: §2.2 Stress, pp. 43-45 (PDF pp. 63-65); abstract p. iv 'a description of the grammar of Tila Chol'

sources.citation: Vázquez Álvarez, Juan Jesús. 2002. Morfología del verbo de la lengua chol de Tila, Chiapas. Tesis de maestría, CIESAS, México. 411 PDF pp. (open PDF, chol.lingspace.org resources page)
sources.quote: 'El acento en el chol recae en la última sílaba de la palabra. En un sólo verbo con sus flexiones podemos observar el movimiento del acento.' Examples (1a-e) wäy-él, wäy-äl-óñ, wäy-äl-oñ-lá, wäy-äl-oñ-bi-lá, wäy-äl-oñ-bi-ka-lá show final stress at 2,3,4,5,6 syllables. 'Sin embargo, el hablante puede darle mayor énfasis acentual a la primera sílaba cuando se interroga' (2a búch-ul, 2b búch-ul-ety=ix). This is the source Coon 2010:190 cites.
sources.locator: §3 'Acento', printed pp. 5-7 (PDF pp. 28-30); also p. 30 fn. 9
